candidates.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
candidates.raw_excerpt: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA . Need for speed The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Chinese researchers have conducted experiments on new wireless communication technology in the Q/V frequency band, achieving a maximum bidirectional transmission rate of 6.75 gigabits per second (Gbps) on a single channel, providing support for the development of 6G communications and satellite internet technology.

As an important frequency band for future 6G communications, the Q/V band offers roughly 10 gigahertz (GHz) of usable bandwidth. With its abundant spectrum resources, it has strong potential for high-speed satellite communications. However, the unique characteristics of millimeter-wave signals in this band make it extremely challenging to achieve high-quality, high-data-rate transmission.

A team from the Aerospace Information Research Institute under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, jointly with other institutions, carried out the communication experiment at a satellite ground station in Lijiang, southwest China's Yunnan Province. The team made key breakthroughs in lightweight antennas, intelligent signal compensation and phase noise compensation, while building a ground-based platform to simulate the in-orbit state of satellites for experimental verification.

The test results showed that the Q/V band achieved a maximum bidirectional transmission rate of 6.75 Gbps on a single channel, which is more than double the rate of existing single-channel transmissions in the same band in China.

The team used dual-carrier and polarization multiplexing technologies to further increase the bidirectional communication rate to 27 Gbps, setting a new record for Q/V-band communication speed in China.

The team said it will continue to improve transmission capabilities, aiming to achieve bidirectional rates exceeding 50 Gbps.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026! When is the best time to look for Leonid meteors? The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere . By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors. Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark. Why are the Leonids special? As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors , which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space.
